\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We measured the cost and answer quality of text, image and combined contexts for multimodal document RAG end to end,
and asked whether a router can use the difference. The answers to the four research questions are as follows.

\emph{RQ1: what the paths cost and how well they answer.} With one shared generator, the page image alone is the
strongest fixed policy, the OCR text path is neither cheap nor accurate, and adding the text to the image costs
1.6$\times$ the GPU time for a small gain. Retrieval misses, not the choice of context, cause most errors:
given the gold page, every path gains far more than any routing policy does.

\emph{RQ2: whether a router can predict the right path before generation.} From the question alone, no: CAVR on
question embeddings is no better than always-visual. Reading what retrieval returned helps. The robust result is a
saving relative to always combining both contexts: CAVR-CE uses 29\% less GPU compute than always-hybrid at
0.008 lower ANLS, and 35\% less on questions from the datasets' training splits, where its ANLS was
no lower. A benefit of query-dependent routing over the best single path is not established: CAVR-CE gained
0.016 ANLS over always-visual for 15\% more compute on the design splits, but only $+0.005$
(interval [-0.004, +0.014]) on the training-split questions, which ColPali and possibly the generator saw in training.
Where the gain appears, it comes from questions whose answer the OCR text helps to read, such as tables and lists on
DocVQA; whether routing beats the best single path depends on how often that happens in a question distribution. A
per-query oracle (ANLS 0.630 at 0.486 GPU-s) shows how much room remains: the bottleneck is predicting
whether a path will succeed.

\emph{RQ3: setting the trade-off and escalating.} The cost weight $\lambda$ is an input of the decision rule, so one
trained router covers a range of budgets; it is a per-deployment setting whose cost estimates must be re-measured on
new hardware. Confidence-based escalation adds nothing beyond it: every escalation operating point lies within
0.010 ANLS of the operating points that lowering $\lambda$ reaches at the same cost.

\emph{RQ4: capacity and index scaling.} Served live with vLLM on one and two A10 GPUs, CAVR-CE sustained
1.82$\times$ the arrival rate of always-hybrid at p95 $\le$ 5\,s on two GPUs, and always-visual
remained ahead of both. A simulator driven by measured service times kept this order but overestimated absolute
capacity by 1.4--2.0$\times$, so the GPU counts it gives for larger pools are projections. Within
a node, sharding exhaustive MaxSim scaled almost linearly, as expected for an embarrassingly parallel search, and an
index of a million pages held in host memory served large batches at close to the throughput per GPU of
GPU-resident search, at 6.4\,s per single query.

All experiments ran within one node, routing and generation on one GPU, and no multi-node experiment was run. Future
work should evaluate routing on document collections with documented non-exposure, serve retrieval, routing and
generation together on a multi-node cluster, widen the path set to the depths and image budgets that lie on the
cost--quality frontier, and improve per-query success prediction.
